Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I think about why the event has happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette: Arthur was nineteen when the shelling tore through his hometown, a sudden rupture of earth and sky that turned a quiet street into a cage of dust and screaming metal. He survived by pressing himself into a damp cellar, the smell of cordite and wet stone lodging deep in his chest. In the decades that followed, he built a steady life, worked as a cashier for forty years, and married a woman who brought warmth into his days. But after she passed, the quiet returned, and with it came the images. They did not arrive as stories; they arrived as stark, unblinking photographs of the cellar's cracked ceiling and the way gray light had bled through the floorboards. When these pictures surfaced, they carried him back to that exact moment, making his heart hammer as though the danger were still closing in. His mind, convinced that the world remained a perpetually hostile place and that he had lost all faith in life's goodness, used those memories as proof that the past was never truly left behind. Each time the past felt present again, Arthur's body braced for an attack, and the sheer intensity of those flashes confirmed his quiet conviction that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. He found himself watching the customers in the checkout lane with intense scrutiny, looking for any twitch that might signal violence, and he stopped sleeping unless he remained propped up with a television playing, convinced that silence meant vulnerability. This unrelenting state of readiness sapped his stamina, which pushed him further into avoiding driving and rejecting positive emotions. To protect himself from the terror of those sudden returns, Arthur simply stopped leaving his house by car. He told himself he no longer needed to travel, though the thought of merging onto a highway made his palms sweat and his breath catch. Over the following months, his avoidance of the car hardened into routine, and by pushing away any positive feelings that tried to surface, he ensured that relief never took root, leaving the old fear to circulate unchecked. The refusal to drive and the deliberate suppression of joy kept his nervous system locked in a low-grade alarm, ensuring that the hypervigilance never truly subsided. Because he spent every waking hour scanning for threat and every sleepless hour guarding against surprise, he found himself increasingly unable to manage the simple logistics of his own life. His inability to engage with the world or allow himself comfort reinforced his conviction that the world was dangerous and that he had lost the capacity to function as he once had. He began searching desperately for meaning in his survival, asking himself why he had been spared while so many others had not, a question that only deepened his isolation. By avoiding driving and rejecting positive emotions, he starved his mind of corrective experiences, which left the old visual fragments floating in isolation, waiting to return and confirm every dark thought he held. At seventy-six, Arthur still stood behind the counter, but the register now felt like a shield against a world that had betrayed him. He came to the clinic because his neighbor finally noticed the unopened mail and the way he flinched when the phone rang, a sight that shattered his last attempt at normalcy. He feared that seeking help would force him to confront the numbness that had kept him alive for decades, yet he hoped, quietly, that someone might finally help him stop watching for ghosts in the checkout line.
